subject: chemistry
question_text: State and explain de Broglie's wave theory.

verification.note: Chapter 1 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.48-52), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+2+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented.

steps.label: The statement
lines: de Broglie's theory: every moving material
particle has wave properties as well as
This is called the dual nature of matter.
steps.why: Light was already known to behave both as a wave and as a particle. de Broglie's step was to say that matter does the same, which is why an electron can be described by a wavelength at all.
common_mistakes: Writing that the particle becomes a wave. It has both natures, it does not change into one.
Leaving out the word moving. A particle at rest has no de Broglie wavelength.
steps.memory_tip: Light behaves as both. de Broglie said matter does too.
steps.margin_note: The words dual nature are worth writing.

steps.label: The equation and its terms
lines: p = mv = momentum of the particle
steps.why: The wavelength is inversely proportional to the momentum, so a heavy or fast particle has a very short wavelength. This single relation is what connects the wave picture to ordinary mechanics.
common_mistakes: Writing λ = mv/h, which turns the relation upside down.
Not naming the symbols. The terms carry marks here as well as the formula.
steps.memory_tip: Wavelength is h divided by momentum. Heavier and faster means shorter.
steps.margin_note: Both marks are here. Write the formula, then name every symbol.

steps.label: Where it applies

lines.text: Significant only for very small particles such as electrons

lines: For a moving cricket ball the mass is large,

steps.why: Because h is extremely small, a measurable wavelength needs a very small mass. The standing-wave condition 2πr = nλ is worth writing because it derives Bohr's quantisation rule instead of assuming it.
common_mistakes: Saying the theory applies to all bodies equally. It applies to all, but is measurable only for small masses.
Leaving out 2πr = nλ, which is the link to the previous chapter's quantisation rule.
steps.memory_tip: The orbit must hold a whole number of waves. That is why n appears at all.
steps.margin_note: The standing-wave line is the part that lifts this answer above a bare formula.

insider_note: The formula alone is half the answer. Writing 2πr = nλ and showing that it gives mvr = nh/2π is what examiners reward, because it explains where Bohr's rule comes from.
